C0.quote: We model the problem as an approval-based multiwinner election
C0.note: Selecting k matchings is modelled as an approval-based (party-approval) multiwinner election with matchings as candidates; voting rules applied.

C1.quote: we establish algorithmic results and axiomatic guarantees that go beyond those
C1.note: Algorithmic results: Lemma 1, Observations 4-5, Theorems 1-4, Corollary 1 (Sections 3.2, 4). Axiomatic results: Theorem 5, Propositions 1-2 (Section 5). Majority of main results are algorithmic/complexity.

C2.1.value: preference profile; approval set; approval preferences
C2.1.quote: a preference profile with Aa ⊆ C denoting the approval set

C2.2.quote: based on the agents’ dichotomous (i.e., approval/disapproval) preferences over each other
C2.2.note: Approval sets over agents, lifted to approval sets over matchings; described as dichotomous preferences.

C2.3.quote: based on the agents’ dichotomous (i.e., approval/disapproval) preferences over each other
C2.3.note: Agents are attributed preferences over each other (approval sets may consist of students they like); these preferences are the input itself, with no separate submitted object.

C2.4.quote: a preference profile with Aa ⊆ C denoting the approval set
C2.4.note: The input is the preference profile; rules are applied directly to it with no statement about reporting or submission.

C3.1.note: No manipulation or strategic analysis; incentive properties mentioned only for Bogomolnaia and Moulin's related work.

C3.2.note: No statement that agents report their true approvals.

C4.1.quote: of (copies of) candidates from W approved by a
C4.1.note: Happiness score h_a(W) is defined as the number of approved candidates in the committee; the paper also uses 'less happy', 'unhappy', 'satisfied' for agents.

C4.2.quote: of (copies of) candidates from W approved by a
C4.2.note: Doubt: the happiness score counts approved matchings (effectively 1 for approved, 0 otherwise), but the intro interprets approval sets only as students one likes or deemed compatible by the teacher; Y chosen as first listed.

C5.1.quote: type of fairness we strive for is captured by proportionality axioms
C5.1.note: Results evaluate rules by proportionality axioms (PJR, EJR, core stability) presented as fairness/representation; Pareto optimality also used in defining candidates.

C5.2.quote: of (copies of) candidates from W approved by a
C5.2.note: Axioms are evaluated via happiness scores computed on the approval profile; no statement relating the profile to separately held attitudes.

VOT.quote_behav: all candidates corresponding to matchings she approves
VOT.note: Agents' approvals are fixed inputs to the rule; no choice of action is modelled.

CAN.note: Candidates are matchings, not acting agents.

C8.1.note: NA: no type is STRAT or MIXED.

claims.quote: finding k matchings fairly representing everyone’s preferences
we can represent the preferences of all agents
the fairness ideal behind the egalitarian solution is not completely satisfactory

C9.1.note: Claims about fairness towards agents and the suitability of proportional rules versus stability, popularity and egalitarian criteria; applications to teachers pairing students, pair programming, shifts in Section 1.

C9.2.note: Fairness to agents' preferences requires that the approval sets used by the rule reflect agents' actual preferences (truthful, non-strategic reporting); not stated. The link between approvals and happiness is stated (happiness score).
